procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal of Lala Ram, dated August 31, 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Hari Ram filed an application under s. 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code for leave to appeal against the Magistrate's order. The High Court granted leave, and Hari Ram filed an appeal. The High Court accepted the appeal, convicted Lala Ram under s. 324, I.P.C., and sentenced him to four months' rigorous imprisonment. Subsequently, an application was filed under s. 561-A, Cr. P.C., read with ss. 3, 4 and 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, but the High Court did not accede to this application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Lala Ram, the appellant, obtained special leave from the Supreme Court to appeal the High Court's judgment.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails and is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether an application for leave to appeal to the High Court under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code was filed within the prescribed limitation period.

facts: An application for leave to appeal an acquittal order dated August 31, 1965, was filed in the High Court on November 1, 1965.
This filing was made after the 60-day period prescribed in Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
The applicant claimed that two days were required to obtain a certified copy of the magistrate's order.
If these two days were deducted from the total time elapsed, the application would be considered within the limitation period.
law: Section 417(4) of the Cr.P.C. states that no application for special leave to appeal an acquittal shall be 'entertained' by the High Court after sixty days from the date of the acquittal order.

Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act allows for the time taken to obtain a certified copy of an order to be excluded when computing the limitation period for an appeal or an application for leave to appeal.
application: The central question was whether the 60-day period in Section 417(4) of the Cr.P.C. is a 'period of limitation' to which Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act can apply.
The appellant argued that Section 417(4) was not a period of limitation but an absolute prohibition that barred the High Court's jurisdiction after 60 days, meaning no deductions could be made.
The Supreme Court rejected this argument, holding that Section 417(4) of the Cr.P.C. does, in fact, prescribe a period of limitation.
The Court reasoned that the legislature was entitled to prescribe a limitation period within the Code itself rather than amending the general Limitation Act.
It classified Section 417(4) as a 'special law' that sets a limitation period for a specific subject (applications for leave to appeal acquittals).
Because the 60-day period was established as a period of limitation, the general rules for computing such periods, including Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, were applicable.
Therefore, the two days the applicant took to obtain the certified copy of the order could be legally deducted from the total time.
With this two-day deduction, the application was considered to have been filed within the 60-day limit.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the application for leave to appeal was filed within the prescribed time. It decided that the 60-day period mentioned in Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code is a period of limitation, which allows for the exclusion of the time taken to obtain a certified copy of the order, as provided under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether the time taken for obtaining a certified copy of the Magistrate's order can be excluded under Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act for an application under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

facts: An application for leave to appeal a Magistrate's order of acquittal, dated August 31, 1965, was filed in the High Court on November 1, 1965.
This filing was beyond the 60-day period prescribed by Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
The applicant claimed that two days were required to obtain a certified copy of the Magistrate's order.
If these two days were excluded from the calculation, the application would be within the time limit.

law.provision: States that no application for special leave to appeal from an order of acquittal shall be entertained by the High Court after the expiry of sixty days from the date of that order.
Stipulates that in computing the period of limitation for an application for leave to appeal, the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the order appealed from shall be excluded.
Makes the provisions of the Limitation Act (like Section 12) applicable to periods of limitation prescribed by any 'special law', unless expressly excluded.

application: The Court first rejected the appellant's argument that Section 417(4) of the Cr.P.C. is a complete jurisdictional bar rather than a period of limitation. The Court held that Section 417(4) itself prescribes a period of limitation, and the legislature is entitled to do so within the Code itself without amending the Limitation Act.

The Court then characterized the limitation period set out in Section 417(4) as a 'special law' of limitation. It reasoned that this period applies only to a specific type of proceeding (applications for special leave to appeal from acquittals) and is therefore a special provision for a special subject.
By classifying Section 417(4) as a 'special law' of limitation, the Court brought it under the purview of Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act.
This made the general provisions of the Limitation Act, including Section 12(2), applicable to the calculation of the 60-day period.
Section 12(2) explicitly allows for the exclusion of time taken to obtain a certified copy of an order when computing the limitation period for an 'application for leave to appeal'.

Since the application under Section 417(3) of the Cr.P.C. is an 'application for leave to appeal', the time taken to obtain the certified copy of the Magistrate's order must be excluded from the 60-day period.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the 60-day period mentioned in Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code is a period of limitation governed by a 'special law'. Consequently, Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act applies, and the time taken to obtain a certified copy of the Magistrate's order must be excluded when calculating the limitation period. Therefore, the application was filed within time.

issue.issue_text: Whether the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act should be extended to the appellant.

facts: The appellant claimed to be under the age of 21 at the time of the offense.
After the High Court delivered its judgment, the appellant filed an application claiming he was 20 years old and should be given the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act.
The High Court rejected this application.
law: Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act provides special considerations for offenders who are under 21 years of age.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the appellant was given an opportunity to prove their age.
However, the appellant failed to provide any "good proof" to establish that they were actually under 21 at the relevant time.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's request for the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act because the appellant failed to furnish sufficient proof of their age, which was a necessary condition for the Act's application.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the finding of fact by the High Court regarding the evidence of the eyewitnesses.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that the High Court should not have interfered with the Magistrate's order of acquittal.
To support this, the counsel took the Supreme Court through the evidence of two eyewitnesses: Poonaram, who was injured, and P.W. 3, Ananda, an independent witness.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence of the two eyewitnesses.
After its review, the Court stated that it agreed with the High Court's assessment that the Magistrate was not entitled to reject the evidence of these witnesses.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided not to interfere with the High Court's finding of fact, stating that the appellant had shown no reason why it should do so.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an application for leave to appeal to the High Court under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code was filed within the prescribed limitation period.
appellant_arguments: The application was filed out of time because Section 417(4) provides a prohibition and bars the High Court's jurisdiction to deal with the application after 60 days have expired.
The word 'entertain' in Section 417(4) means 'to deal with or hear', not just 'file or receive', meaning the application would be barred if not heard within 60 days.
respondent_arguments: The application was filed within the prescribed time because the two days taken to obtain a certified copy of the Magistrate's order should be deducted from the total period.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the time taken for obtaining a certified copy of the Magistrate's order can be excluded under Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act for an application under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
appellant_arguments: Section 12(2) of the Indian Limitation Act is not attracted to applications under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code, so the time for obtaining a certified copy cannot be excluded.
respondent_arguments: The applicant was entitled to deduct the two days taken for obtaining the certified copy of the Magistrate's order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act should be extended to the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, being 20 years old, should have been given the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not detailed in the provided text, but their position is implied by the High Court's rejection of the appellant's application on this matter.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the finding of fact by the High Court regarding the evidence of the eyewitnesses.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should not have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the Magistrate.
No offence was committed because the accused had a right of private defence of property.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not detailed, but their position, upheld by the court, was that the High Court was correct to convict as the Magistrate was not entitled to reject the evidence of the eyewitnesses.

cases.principle: The 60-day limitation period prescribed in s. 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code for an application for special leave to appeal from an order of acquittal is a 'special law' within the meaning of s. 29(2) of the Limitation Act.
Cited in support of the proposition that s. 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code prescribes a period of limitation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The right of private defence of property is not available when there is ample opportunity to have recourse to the authorities.
obiter: The 60-day limitation period for an application under s.417(3) of the Code is a special law of limitation provided for within the Code itself.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that an application for leave to appeal under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code was filed within the prescribed time limit. The word "entertain" in Section 417(4) means "file or receive by the court" and does not refer to the actual hearing of the application. The Court also declined to interfere with the High Court's findings of fact regarding the evidence and the rejection of the private defense claim, and denied the appellant the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act due to a lack of proof of age.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation of the word 'entertain' within the context of Section 417(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
Assessment of the right of private defense, considering whether the accused had an opportunity to have recourse to public authorities.
Evidentiary standard for establishing age to claim the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act.
why_appellant_lost: The Court interpreted the word 'entertain' in s. 417(4) to mean 'file or receive by the Court' and not 'to deal with or hear', thus rejecting the argument that the High Court's jurisdiction was barred because the application was not heard within 60 days.
The appellant failed to furnish good proof to establish that he was under the age of 21 at the relevant time, and therefore could not be extended the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act.

The claim of a right of private defense of property was dismissed on the grounds that, even assuming such a right existed, the appellant had ample opportunity to have recourse to the authorities and there was no need to take the law into his own hands.

The appellant showed no reason why the Supreme Court should interfere with the finding of fact arrived at by the High Court, which found that the Magistrate was not entitled to reject the evidence of the eyewitnesses.
why_respondent_won: The application for leave to appeal was deemed to be within the time limit because the court adopted a practical interpretation of 'entertain' as meaning the date of filing, which prevented applications from being time-barred due to court scheduling delays.
The High Court's conviction was upheld because the Supreme Court saw no reason to interfere with its finding of fact based on the evidence of the eyewitnesses.
policy_considerations: If 'entertain' were interpreted to mean the actual hearing of the application, the result would be that in many cases applications for leave to appeal would be barred simply because the applications have not been put up for hearing before the High Court within sixty days of the order of acquittal.
